paras: The whipping of Dorritt Banks was the public thrashing of a Black youth by a white man in the upper part of Greenville County, South Carolina, in early March 1881. Accused of forcibly kissing a white schoolgirl, Banks was whipped by her father before witnesses after Banks's father chose the thrashing over a prosecution. A Greenville dispatch printed in the Chicago Daily Tribune presented the case as an example of a "novel" and "economical" way of punishing crime.

According to the dispatch, dated March 5, a group of white schoolgirls was walking home in the upper part of the county on the afternoon of March 4. Banks, described as a "colored youth," was accused of ordering the girls to halt, seizing the tallest of them and forcibly kissing her on the cheek. The girl went home and told her father of what the dispatch called "the indignity."

The father went at once to the Banks house and offered the youth's father a choice between a public thrashing of the boy and a criminal prosecution. The thrashing was accepted, the boy was "secured," and the girl's father whipped him before the whole household and several neighbors who gathered to watch. Beyond a phrase about making "the woodland echoes ring," the dispatch did not say exactly where the whipping took place or describe any injuries.
No report of an arrest or official action appears in the coverage, and no statement from Banks or his family was printed.

The only report found ran in the Chicago Daily Tribune on March 8, 1881, under the headline "Flogging Negroes. The Novel Method of Punishing Crime Adopted in South Carolina." Told from the white side, the dispatch treated the accusation as fact and called Banks "the assailant." It paired the case with a flogging at Greenville a day or two earlier, in which a Black man accused of stealing a ham agreed with a merchant to take thirty-one blows on his bare back, and concluded that the State had been saved the expense of prosecution while "all parties were perfectly satisfied."

accounts.label: Greenville dispatch
accounts.gist: Banks halted a group of white schoolgirls and forcibly kissed one; her father, given the choice by Banks's father, whipped the youth publicly instead of prosecuting him. The account comes only from the white side and gives no statement from Banks or his family.

framing.detail: The Chicago Daily Tribune ran the Greenville dispatch as 'Flogging Negroes,' calling the method 'novel' and 'economical,' treating the accusation as fact ('the indignity,' 'the negro had insulted') and closing that 'all parties were perfectly satisfied' in the companion case.
